subject: math
title: Grade 6 Probability: Theoretical and Experimental
seo_title: Grade 6 Probability Worksheets: Free Math Practice with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Single-outcome probability, both theoretical and experimental
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 math worksheets on probability for the BC curriculum: probability as a fraction, decimal and percent, theoretical probability with number cubes and spinners, experimental probability from results, comparing the two, and fair games. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Theoretical probability = outcomes you want ÷ all the outcomes. Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ number of trials.
key_sub: On a number cube, “greater than 4” is 5 and 6 only: 2/6. With more trials, the experimental probability usually gets closer to the theory. A game is fair when every player has the same chance.
body_html:
What is a probability?

A probability is a number from 0 to 1. 0 means impossible. 1 means certain. 12 (0.5) means equally likely to happen or not. A probability is never more than 1.

You can write the same probability as a fraction, a decimal or a percent.

FractionDecimalPercentChance
000%impossible
140.2525%unlikely
120.550%equally likely
340.7575%likely
11100%certain

Theoretical probability

Theoretical probability is what should happen. When the outcomes are equally likely:

probability = outcomes you want ÷ all the possible outcomes

Example 1

You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?

Greater than 4 means 5 or 6. That is 2 of the 6 outcomes. Do not count the 4.

Answer: 26 = 13

Example 2

What is the probability of landing on blue?

Blue is one quarter of the spinner. Do not count colours (1 of 3), because the sections are not equal.

Answer: 14 = 0.25 = 25%

Experimental probability

Experimental probability is what did happen in an experiment:

experimental probability = times it happened ÷ number of trials

Example 3

What is the experimental probability of red?

Red came up 11 times in 20 spins. The theory says 12 = 0.5, so the result is close.

Answer: 1120 = 0.55 = 55%

Theoretical and experimental probabilities are usually close, but rarely exactly the same. More trials usually get closer to the theory.

Coin tossesHeadsExperimental probability
107710 = 0.7
1004646100 = 0.46
10005085081000 = 0.508

Fair games

A game is fair when every player has the same probability of winning.

Example 4

On a number cube, Liam wins on 1 or 2 and Ava wins on 3, 4, 5 or 6. Is the game fair?

Liam: 26. Ava: 46. The probabilities are not equal.

Answer: No, Ava is more likely to win

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
3 red, 5 blue, so P(red) = 35.Divide by ALL the outcomes: 38.
3 colours, so each colour is 13.Only if the sections are the same size.
“Greater than 4” includes the 4.Greater than 4 on a number cube means 5 and 6 only.
“5 tails in a row, so heads is due.”A coin has no memory. Heads is still 12.

faq.q: What do Grade 6 students learn about probability in BC?
faq.a: The BC Grade 6 math curriculum covers single-outcome probability, both theoretical and experimental. Students write probabilities as fractions, decimals and percents, find them for number cubes and spinners, compare them with results from experiments, and decide whether games are fair.

faq.q: What is the difference between theoretical and experimental probability?
faq.a: Theoretical probability is what should happen, found by counting outcomes: a 6 on a number cube is 1/6. Experimental probability is what actually happened, such as 23 heads in 50 tosses (23/50). With more trials, the two usually get closer.

faq.q: How do you know if a game is fair?
faq.a: A game is fair when every player has the same probability of winning. On a number cube, 1, 2, 3 against 4, 5, 6 is fair (3/6 each), but 1, 2 against 3, 4, 5, 6 is not (2/6 against 4/6).

faq.q: Why is the experimental probability different from the theoretical probability?
faq.a: Each trial depends on chance, so results vary, especially with only a few trials. If you toss a coin 10 times you might get 7 heads, but after 1000 tosses the share of heads is usually very close to 1/2.

sets.title: Probability as a fraction, decimal and percent

items.q: What is the probability of an event that is impossible?
items.e: An impossible event can never happen, so its probability is 0. 0.1 is very unlikely, but it can still happen.

items.q: What is the probability of an event that is certain?
items.e: A certain event will happen, so its probability is 1 (or 100%). The number 100 on its own is far bigger than 1, so it can’t be a probability.

items.q: An event is equally likely to happen or not happen. What is its probability?
items.e: Equally likely is halfway between 0 and 1: 12 (0.5 or 50%). 2 is the number of outcomes, not the probability.

items.q: Which number can NOT be a probability?
items.e: Probabilities go from 0 to 1. 1.5 is bigger than 1, so it can’t be a probability. 0 and 1 are allowed: they mean impossible and certain.

items.q: Which percent can NOT be a probability?
items.e: As a percent, probabilities go from 0% to 100%. 120% is more than 100%, so it is not possible.

items.q: Which word best describes the chance shown by the arrow?
items.e: The arrow is at 0.8. That is between 0.5 and 1, close to 1: likely. It is not certain, because it is not at 1.

items.q: The probability of heads is 12. What is this as a decimal?
items.e: 12 = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5. Writing the digits 1 and 2 as 0.12 or 1.2 is a common mistake.

items.q: The probability of landing on blue is 14. What is this as a percent?
items.e: 14 = 25100 = 25%. 14% just writes the digits 1 and 4.

items.q: Write the probability 310 as a decimal.
items.e: 310 is 3 tenths = 0.3. 0.03 is 3 hundredths.

items.q: Write the probability 0.75 as a percent.
items.e: To change a decimal to a percent, multiply by 100: 0.75 × 100 = 75%. 25% is the chance that the event does NOT happen.

items.q: Which fraction is equal to the probability 0.2?
items.e: 0.2 = 210 = 15. 12 is 0.5, and 2100 is 0.02.

items.q: Write the probability 35 as a percent.
items.e: 35 = 60100 = 60%. Multiply the numerator and denominator by 20. 35% just writes the digits 3 and 5.

items.q: Write the probability 40% as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.e: 40% = 40100. Divide the numerator and denominator by 20: 25. 4100 would be 4%.

items.q: Write the probability 0.05 as a percent.
Write the probability 18 as a decimal.
items.e: 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125 (125 thousandths). A quick check: 14 = 0.25, and 18 is half of that.

items.q: Write the probability 720 as a percent.
items.e: Multiply the numerator and denominator by 5: 720 = 35100 = 35%. 27% comes from adding 7 + 20.

items.q: The line is split into tenths. What probability does the arrow show, as a percent?
items.e: The arrow is 3 small steps from 0, at 0.3. 0.3 = 30 hundredths = 30%. 70% counts back from 1. 3% would be 0.03.

items.q: Which shows the probability of landing on blue as a fraction, a decimal and a percent?
items.e: Blue covers one quarter of the spinner: 14 = 0.25 = 25%. 12 is the probability of red. 14 is 0.25, not 0.4 or 0.14.

items.q: Which probability is the greatest?
items.e: Change them all to decimals: 34 = 0.75, 0.7 = 0.70, 72% = 0.72, 0.69. The greatest is 34.

items.q: The forecast for Vancouver says there is a 70% chance of rain tomorrow. What is this probability as a decimal?
items.e: 70% = 70100 = 0.7. Divide by 100 to change a percent to a decimal. 0.3 is the chance of NO rain.

sets.title: Theoretical probability: number cubes and spinners

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a 4?
items.e: There are 6 equally likely outcomes and only one of them is 4: 16. 46 would be the chance of 1, 2, 3 or 4.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling an even number?
items.e: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6: 3 of the 6 outcomes, so 36 (= 12). 63 is upside down: it is greater than 1.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
items.e: Greater than 4 means 5 or 6: 2 of the 6 outcomes, so 26. 36 wrongly includes the 4. 16 forgets the 5.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a number less than 5?
items.e: Less than 5 means 1, 2, 3 or 4: 4 of the 6 outcomes, so 46. 56 wrongly includes the 5. 26 counts the outcomes you don’t want (5 and 6).

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a multiple of 3?
items.e: The multiples of 3 on the cube are 3 and 6: 26. 36 also counts 9, which is not on the cube. 16 forgets the 6.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of rolling a prime number?
items.e: The prime numbers are 2, 3 and 5: 36. 46 wrongly counts 1, which is not prime. 26 forgets that 2 is prime.

items.q: You roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. What is the probability of NOT rolling a 6?
items.e: Not a 6 means 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5: 56. Check: 56 + 16 = 1. 65 is upside down and greater than 1.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on red?
items.e: Red covers half of the spinner: 12. 13 counts the 3 colours, but the sections are not the same size.

items.q: The spinner has 8 equal sections: G is green and Y is yellow. What is the probability of green?
items.e: 3 of the 8 equal sections are green: 38. 35 compares green with yellow, not with all 8 sections. 58 is yellow.

items.q: A spinner has 10 equal sections: 3 blue and 7 red. What is the probability of blue as a decimal?
items.e: 3 of the 10 sections are blue: 310 = 0.3. 0.7 is the probability of red.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on a prime number?
items.e: The prime numbers are 2, 3, 5 and 7: 4 of the 8 sections, so 48 (= 12). 58 wrongly counts 1, which is not prime. 38 forgets 2.

items.q: Red is in two small parts, each one eighth of the spinner. What is the probability of red?
items.e: 18 + 18 = 28 = 14. 25 counts 2 of the 5 sections, but the sections are not the same size.

items.q: On which spinner is the probability of blue 14?
items.e: On spinner C, blue has 2 of the 8 equal sections: 28 = 14. A has 4 colours, but blue is half of it. B is 13 and D is 34.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on a multiple of 4, as a percent?
items.e: The multiples of 4 are 4 and 8: 210 = 20100 = 20%. 2% uses the count as the percent. 40% counts every number up to 4. 25% comes from thinking “4 means 14”.

items.q: A 12-sided die has the numbers 1 to 12. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 9?
items.e: Greater than 9 means 10, 11 or 12: 312 (= 14). 412 wrongly includes the 9. 912 is the chance of 1 to 9, the numbers you don’t want.

items.q: The spinner has 5 equal sections. What is the probability of red, as a decimal?
items.e: 3 of the 5 equal sections are red: 35 = 610 = 0.6. 0.35 just writes the digits 3 and 5. 1.5 compares red with not red (3 ÷ 2).

items.q: Simran says the probability of yellow is 14 because there are 4 colours. What is the probability of yellow?
items.e: The colours are not the same size. Yellow is half of a quarter: 18. Counting colours only works when every section is the same size.

items.q: A special number cube has the faces 1, 1, 2, 2, 2 and 3. What is the probability of rolling a 2?
items.e: The cube has 6 faces and 3 of them show a 2: 36 (= 12). 13 counts the 3 different numbers, but they are not on the same number of faces. 33 compares the faces with a 2 with the other 3 faces.

items.q: Each letter of OKANAGAN is on a card. The cards are mixed up and turned over. You pick one card. What is the probability of A?
items.e: There are 8 cards and 3 of them show A: 38. 15 counts the 5 different letters (O, K, A, N, G), but A is on 3 cards. 35 compares the A cards with the other 5 cards.

items.q: What is the probability of landing on an even number that is greater than 3?
items.e: Even and greater than 3: 4, 6 and 8. That is 38. 48 counts every even number, with 2. 28 forgets the 8. 58 counts every number greater than 3.

items.q: Ryan tosses a coin 50 times and gets 23 heads. What is the experimental probability of heads?
items.e: Experimental probability = number of times it happened ÷ number of trials = 2350. 12 is the theoretical probability. 2327 compares heads with tails.

items.q: Which sentence describes experimental probability?
c: The number of trials ÷ the number of times it happened
The number of times it happened
The number of times it happened ÷ the number of trials
The outcomes you want ÷ all the possible outcomes
items.e: Experimental probability comes from what happened in an experiment: times it happened ÷ number of trials. Counting the possible outcomes gives the theoretical probability.

items.q: Nadia’s class recorded 20 spins. What is the experimental probability of red, as a decimal?
items.e: Red came up 12 times in 20 spins: 1220 = 610 = 0.6. 1.5 comes from 12 ÷ 8 (red ÷ blue), and it is greater than 1.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of yellow, as a percent?
items.e: Yellow came up 10 times in 40 spins: 1040 = 14 = 25%. 10% uses the count as the percent. 30% is blue.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of rolling a 4?
items.e: The tally for 4 shows 3 rolls out of 30: 330. 16 is the theoretical probability. 430 uses the number 4 instead of its frequency.

items.q: At hockey practice, Harjot scored on 8 of his 25 shots. What is his experimental probability of scoring, as a percent?
items.e: 825 = 32100 = 32% (multiply the numerator and denominator by 4). 8% uses the count as the percent. 68% is the shots he missed.

items.q: Ethan counts 40 cars passing the school in Burnaby. 14 of them are white. Estimate the probability that the next car is white.
items.e: 14 ÷ 40 = 35100 = 0.35. 0.14 uses the count as the decimal. 0.65 is the estimate for a car that is NOT white.

items.q: In Vancouver last November, it rained on 21 of the 30 days. What is the experimental probability of rain on a November day, as a decimal?
items.e: 2130 = 710 = 0.7. 0.21 uses the count as the decimal. 0.3 is the dry days.

items.q: Kai takes a marble from a bag, records its colour and puts it back. He does this 50 times. What is the experimental probability of NOT red?
items.e: Not red means blue or green: 18 + 10 = 28 of the 50 draws, so 2850. 2250 is red. 1050 counts only green.

items.q: Owen flips a bottle cap 80 times. It lands top-up 36 times. What is the experimental probability of top-up, as a percent?
items.e: 3680 = 920 = 45100 = 45%. 36% uses the count as the percent. 55% is top-down. 44% comes from 80 − 36.

items.q: Chloe spins a spinner 25 times and gets green 9 times. What is the experimental probability of green, as a decimal?
items.e: 925 = 36100 = 0.36. 0.09 and 0.9 just use the 9. 0.64 is the probability of NOT green.

items.q: Leah takes 15 penalty kicks at soccer practice and scores 6 times. What is her experimental probability of scoring, as a decimal?
items.e: 615 = 25 = 0.4. 0.6 is the kicks she missed. 0.06 uses the count as the decimal.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of blue or green?
items.e: Blue or green: 11 + 8 = 19 of the 30 spins, so 1930. 24 counts 2 of the 4 colours, but experimental probability uses the results.

items.q: Zara’s school bus in Kelowna was late on 4 of the 20 school days in February. What is the experimental probability that the bus is late, in lowest terms?
items.e: 420 = 15. 14 compares the 4 late days with the 16 on-time days. 45 is the chance it is on time.

items.q: Jasleen spins a spinner and gets red 12 times. Her experimental probability of red is 310. How many times did she spin?
items.e: 310 = 1240, so she spun 40 times. 36 comes from 12 × 3. 30 comes from 3 × 10.

items.q: After 40 coin tosses, Wei’s experimental probability of heads is 0.45. How many heads did he get?
items.e: 0.45 × 40 = 18. Check: 1840 = 45100 = 0.45. 20 is half of 40 (the theory). 22 is the number of tails.

items.q: On a field trip to a salmon hatchery, students count 200 young salmon. 130 of them are coho. Estimate the probability that the next salmon counted is coho, as a percent.
items.e: 130200 = 65100 = 65%. 130% is more than 100%, so it can’t be a probability. 35% is NOT coho.

items.q: A bag has 20 marbles. Sofia takes one, records its colour and puts it back. She does this 100 times and gets red 26 times. About how many red marbles are in the bag?
items.e: Red came up 26100 = 0.26 of the time, about a quarter. 14 of 20 is 5, so there are about 5 red marbles. 26 is more than the whole bag.

items.q: Three groups spin the same spinner 20 times each. Red comes up 9, 13 and 8 times. Use all the results to estimate the probability of red.
items.e: Add the results: 9 + 13 + 8 = 30 reds in 3 × 20 = 60 spins. 3060 (= 12). Using all 60 spins gives a better estimate than one group. 3020 is greater than 1.

items.q: Four friends practise basketball shots. Noah: 12 baskets in 20 shots. Ava: 15 in 30. Lucas: 7 in 10. Zara: 18 in 40. Who has the greatest experimental probability of scoring?
items.e: Noah 1220 = 0.6, Ava 1530 = 0.5, Lucas 710 = 0.7, Zara 1840 = 0.45. Lucas is greatest. Zara made the most baskets, but she also took the most shots.

items.q: Liam rolls a number cube 60 times. About how many times would he expect to roll a 6?
items.e: A 6 has a theoretical probability of 16. 16 of 60 is 60 ÷ 6 = 10, so about 10.

items.q: Emma tosses a coin 100 times. How many heads should she expect?
items.e: Half of 100 is 50. Results change from one experiment to the next, so expect about 50, not exactly 50.

items.q: Lucas spins this spinner 40 times. About how many times should he expect red?
items.e: Red is 34 of the spinner. 40 ÷ 4 = 10, and 3 × 10 = 30, so about 30. About 10 is for blue.

items.q: A spinner has 4 equal sections, and one is blue. Olivia spins it 40 times and gets blue 13 times. How does the experimental probability of blue compare with the theoretical probability?
c: 1340 is less than 14
1340 is a little greater than 14
1327 is much greater than 14
items.e: Experimental: 1340 = 0.325. Theoretical: 14 = 0.25. So 1340 is a little greater than 14. 1327 compares blue with not blue.

items.q: Ava tosses a coin 10 times and gets 7 heads. Noah tosses a coin 1000 times and gets 508 heads. Whose experimental probability of heads is closer to 12?
items.e: Ava: 710 = 0.7. Noah: 5081000 = 0.508. 0.508 is much closer to 0.5, so Noah’s is closer.

items.q: Why are Noah’s results (1000 tosses) closer to 12 than Ava’s (10 tosses)?
c: Noah tossed the coin more carefully
Big experiments are always exactly right
More trials usually get closer to the theory
items.e: With only a few trials, luck changes the results a lot. More trials usually get closer to the theoretical probability, but not exactly.

items.q: How do these results compare with the theory?
c: 4 will come up more next time
The number cube must be unfair
Close: each number should come up about 10 times
items.e: Theory: 16 of 60 = 10 for each number. The results are all between 8 and 12, which is close to the theory. Small differences are normal.

items.q: Leah rolls a number cube 600 times and gets a 6 on 104 rolls. How does this compare with the theory?
items.e: 16 of 600 = 600 ÷ 6 = 100. 104 is close to 100. Experiments are rarely exactly the same as the theory.

items.q: A computer simulates tossing a coin 10 000 times. About how many heads would you expect?
items.e: Half of 10 000 is 5000. A simulation with many trials gets close to the theory, so expect about 5000, not exactly 5000.

items.q: A spinner has 4 equal sections: red, blue, yellow and green. At a school fun fair in Surrey, red comes up 98 times in 200 spins. What do the results suggest?
c: 200 spins are too few to tell
The spinner is probably not fair
Red will stop coming up soon
items.e: Theory: 14 of 200 = 50 reds. 98 is almost double that, after many spins, so the spinner is probably not fair.

items.q: Hana rolls a number cube 50 times and gets an even number 33 times. How much greater is the experimental probability of an even number than the theoretical probability, as a decimal?
items.e: Experimental: 3350 = 0.66. Theoretical: 36 = 0.5. 0.66 − 0.5 = 0.16. 0.17 comes from 50 − 33 = 17.

items.q: Before each lacrosse game, a coin is tossed to decide which team starts. Tails has come up 5 games in a row. What is the probability of heads at the next game?
items.e: The coin has no memory. Every toss is a new trial, so heads is still 12. Thinking heads is “due” is called the gambler’s fallacy.

items.q: Kai has rolled a number cube 12 times without getting a 6. What is the probability of a 6 on the next roll?
items.e: The number cube does not remember earlier rolls. A 6 is still 16. It is not certain (1), even after a long wait.

items.q: Ji-woo spins a spinner with 5 equal sections, each a different colour, 50 times. In theory, about how many times should each colour come up?
items.e: Each colour has a probability of 15. 15 of 50 is 50 ÷ 5 = 10. About 5 confuses the 5 sections with the answer.

items.q: Four groups each spin a spinner with 4 equal sections 80 times. They get red 19, 30, 12 and 40 times (Groups A, B, C and D). Whose result is closest to the theory?
items.e: Theory: 14 of 80 = 20 reds. Group A’s 19 is only 1 away, so Group A is closest. Group D’s 40 would be the theory for half of the spinner.

items.q: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue marbles. Arjun takes a marble, records its colour and puts it back, 50 times. About how many reds should he expect?
items.e: Red is 3 of 10 marbles: 310. 310 of 50 = 15. About 35 is for blue. About 21 comes from 37 (red compared with blue).

items.q: Simran tosses a coin 500 times and gets 262 heads. What is the experimental probability of heads, as a decimal?
items.e: 262500 = 5241000 = 0.524, close to the theoretical 0.5. 0.476 is tails. 0.262 uses the count as a decimal.

items.q: Mateo spins a spinner 100 times: red 52, blue 23, yellow 25. Which spinner did he most likely use?
items.e: Red came up about half the time, and blue and yellow about a quarter each. Spinner B is 12 red, 14 blue and 14 yellow. A would give about 33 of each.

items.q: Wei spins a spinner 50 times and gets blue 20 times. Use his experimental probability to predict how many blues he will get in 200 spins.
items.e: 2050 = 25. 25 of 200 = 80. Or: 200 is 4 × 50, so 4 × 20 = 80. About 40 only doubles the 20.

items.q: Mateo rolls a number cube once and gets a 6. He says, “The experimental probability of a 6 is 1, so this cube always lands on 6.” What is the best answer?
c: He is right, the cube always lands on 6
One roll is too few trials to tell
The probability of a 6 is now 0
He should use 66 instead
items.e: With only one trial, the experimental probability can be far from the theory (16). He needs many more rolls to tell if the cube is fair.

items.q: Liam and Olivia toss a coin. Liam wins on heads and Olivia wins on tails. Is the game fair?
c: Yes, each has a probability of 12
No, Liam is more likely to win
No, Olivia is more likely to win
items.e: A game is fair when every player has the same probability of winning. Heads and tails are both 12, so yes.

items.q: Arjun and Chloe roll a number cube. Arjun wins on 1 or 2. Chloe wins on 3, 4, 5 or 6. Is the game fair?
c: No, Arjun is more likely to win
Yes, each has 12
Yes, they each have a number
No, Chloe is more likely to win
items.e: Arjun: 26. Chloe: 46. The chances are not equal, so no, Chloe is more likely to win.

items.q: Noah and Ava roll a number cube. Noah wins on an even number and Ava wins on an odd number. What is Ava’s probability of winning?
items.e: The odd numbers are 1, 3 and 5: 36. Noah also has 36 (2, 4, 6), so the game is fair. 33 compares Ava’s numbers with Noah’s.

items.q: Mei and Lucas roll a number cube. Mei wins on a prime number. Lucas wins on a number that is not prime. What is Lucas’s probability of winning?
items.e: Not prime: 1, 4 and 6 (1 is not a prime number). That is 36. 26 forgets the 1. 46 thinks 2 is not prime. So the game is fair.

items.q: Kai wins if the spinner lands on red. Zara wins if it lands on blue or yellow. Is the game fair?
c: Yes, each has 12
No, Kai is more likely to win
No, Zara has 23
items.e: Kai: red = 12. Zara: 14 + 14 = 12. Yes, it is fair. Counting colours (1 against 2) is the mistake.

items.q: Owen wins on red, Leah wins on blue and Ryan wins on yellow. Who is most likely to win?
items.e: Owen’s red is 12 of the spinner. Leah and Ryan have 14 each. Owen is most likely to win, so the game is not fair.

items.q: Wei, Hana and Mateo roll a number cube. Wei wins on 1 or 2, Hana on 3 or 4, and Mateo on 5 or 6. What is each player’s probability of winning?
items.e: Each player has 2 of the 6 numbers: 26 (= 13). The three chances are equal, so the game is fair.

items.q: A spinner has 8 equal sections: 5 blue and 3 red. Ethan wins on blue and Sofia wins on red. Which change makes the game fair?
items.e: A fair spinner needs 4 blue and 4 red sections. Painting 1 blue section red gives 48 each. Painting 2 would give 3 blue and 5 red: unfair the other way.

items.q: A bag has 4 green and 6 yellow marbles. Jasleen wins if she takes a green marble. What is her probability of winning?
items.e: 4 of the 10 marbles are green: 410. 46 compares green with yellow. 12 counts 2 colours, but there are more yellow marbles.

items.q: The bag has 4 green and 6 yellow marbles. Jasleen wins on green and Harjot wins on yellow. How many green marbles should be added to make the game fair?
items.e: Fair means the same number of green and yellow marbles: 6 green and 6 yellow. 6 − 4 = 2. Adding 6 would make 10 green. 1 would only work if you also took out a yellow one.

items.q: Ryan and Nadia roll a number cube. Ryan gets points on a 6. Nadia gets 1 point on any other number. How many points should Ryan get for a 6 to make the game fair?
items.e: Nadia wins 56 of the rolls and Ryan only 16, 5 times less often. So Ryan should get 5 points. In 60 rolls: Ryan 10 × 5 = 50, Nadia 50 × 1 = 50.

items.q: A prize wheel at a school carnival in Kamloops has 10 equal sections. 2 sections win a prize. What is the probability of winning a prize, as a percent?
items.e: 210 = 20100 = 20%. 80% is the chance of NOT winning. 25% compares the 2 prize sections with the other 8.

items.q: A class sells 200 raffle tickets to raise money for the Terry Fox Run. Harjot buys 5 tickets. One ticket is drawn. What is the probability that Harjot wins, as a percent?
items.e: 5200 = 140 = 0.025 = 2.5%. 5% uses the number of tickets as the percent.

items.q: Game A: spin a spinner with 3 equal sections and win on red. Game B: pick a ticket from a box of 10 tickets where 3 tickets win. Which game gives a better chance of winning?
c: Game B, it has more winning tickets
items.e: Game A: 13 ≈ 0.333. Game B: 310 = 0.3. Game A is a little better, even though Game B has more winning tickets.

items.q: Cards numbered 1 to 10 are mixed up. Nadia wins if she picks a number less than 5. Owen wins if she picks a number greater than 5. Who is more likely to win?
items.e: Less than 5: 1, 2, 3, 4 (4 cards). Greater than 5: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 (5 cards). Owen has 510 and Nadia 410. Counting 1 to 5 and 5 to 10 as 5 each is the mistake.

items.q: Kai and Leah play a fair coin game 20 times. Kai wins 13 games. Does this show that the game is unfair?
c: Yes, Kai is more likely to win
No, the results must be 10 and 10
No, 20 games is too few to tell
Yes, Leah’s chance is now 720
items.e: In theory each player wins 12 of the time, but results vary. 13 wins in only 20 games can happen by chance. No, 20 games is too few to tell.

items.q: Wei, Mei and Nadia spin a spinner with 4 equal sections: red, blue, yellow and green. Wei wins on red, Mei on blue, and Nadia on yellow or green. What is Nadia’s probability of winning?
items.e: Nadia has 2 of the 4 equal sections: 24. 13 uses the 3 players, but the outcomes are the 4 sections. The game is not fair.

items.q: A spinner at a ski lodge in Whistler has 12 equal sections. 3 sections win a free hot chocolate. What is the probability of NOT winning, as a decimal?
items.e: Not winning: 12 − 3 = 9 sections. 912 = 34 = 0.75. 0.25 is the chance of winning. 0.9 just uses the 9.

items.q: Arjun and Simran roll a number cube. Which rule makes a fair game?
c: Arjun wins on 1 or 2; Simran wins on 3, 4, 5 or 6
Arjun wins on 1 or 6; Simran wins on 2, 3 or 4
Arjun wins on 1, 2 or 3; Simran wins on 4, 5 or 6
Arjun wins on 5; Simran wins on any other number
items.e: In a fair game both players have the same number of outcomes. 1, 2 or 3 against 4, 5 or 6 gives each 36. With 1 or 6 against 2, 3 or 4, the 5 wins for nobody and Simran has more.

items.q: Owen gets 1 point when the spinner lands on red. Leah gets points when it lands on blue. How many points should Leah get for blue to make the game fair?
items.e: Red is 34 and blue is 14: red comes up 3 times as often. So Leah needs 3 points. In 40 spins: Owen 30 × 1 = 30, Leah 10 × 3 = 30. 4 counts all 4 quarters.
